item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
The compute needed for the stage of AI we’re about to enter is going to be insane.
Personal agents, agent swarms defending enterprises, agents that review all of our code for security issues, agents that process nearly all enterprise data in workflows, background agents working on tasks 24/7, and on and on.
This will take a mix of inference volume that is going to keep growing by orders of magnitude, as well as infrastructure that agents need alongside the tokens. They need computers, networking, file systems, and so on.
We’re only in the early stages of what this buildout is going to look like.

There are real costs in every direction: time, attention, opportunity. You...
item.description:
作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
One thing the engineering community will (re)discover is that every program can be ① hardened (edge cases squashed, inputs tightened, errors handled) and ② optimized (profiled, benchmarked, rewritten) basically ad infinitum.
There are real costs in every direction: time, attention, opportunity. You can literally explore input spaces that will never be hit or optimize performance of something that will never be used ("you have no users".) Even in an infinite token world, you need to know when to stop and what tradeoffs to accept. Agents will happily drill no matter what.

item.title: OpenAI’s Dots launched last week and they've taken over @every. A few things that stand out: They protect your attention. Over the weekend, my Dot posted my model-testing results to Slack and brought back replies. I could keep working without opening Slack and disappearing down a rabbit hole. My w...
item.description:
作者：Dan Shipper 账号：@danshipper 简介：ceo @every | the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI
OpenAI’s Dots launched last week and they've taken over @every.
A few things that stand out:
They protect your attention. Over the weekend, my Dot posted my model-testing results to Slack and brought back replies. I could keep working without opening Slack and disappearing down a rabbit hole. My weekend stayed pretty clear and calm.
They’re useful for the little things you miss. People at Every are using them to pull important information out of school emails, catch missed Slack messages, and flag account-access requests.
Voice makes them useful away from your laptop. Our head of video was talking his Dot through video edits while running around getting our launch out.
The ecosystem matters. Dots feel roughly at feature parity with Muse, Instinct, and Grok bots. But having an agent connected to the ecosystem you already use for work and life is a real advantage. If you use ChatGPT, I recommend trying one.
Permissions are still frustrating. I have to approve the same basic thing multiple times, and sometimes even after I approve it, my Dot says it can’t do it. That needs to get fixed.
I’m less convinced we’ll stay loyal to the characters. Mine is named Boo, and I’m attached to him. But I felt that way about my OpenClaw agent, too. When something better comes along, I switch. In a year, I expect to be using a persistent agent. Boo will probably be dead. RIP, Boo.
I get into all of this at the start of this week’s podcast, and then sit down with @bigwilliestyle to talk about where we go from here.
In a lot of ways, Dots and GrokBots remind me of a wave we went through with OpenClaw eight months ago. We talk about personal vs. company agents, why we built our own company agent, and whether companies will end up with a whole shadow org chart of agents.
Full episode below.

item.title: Why Every Traded Personal Agents for One Company Agent
item.description:
播客：AI & I by Every
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:12 The hot thing right now is dots. They're persistent agents from OpenAI. I was there at Dev Day when they launched them. I interviewed Sam about them, and I've been using dots since before they came out. And now we're into week two of dots.
Speaker 1 | 00:12 - 00:46 So how's it going? If you read my vibe check, you know that I thought they were a little bit rough to begin with, but that the idea of a persistent proactive agent was obviously the future. Even before DOTS launched, they'd become my main way of interacting with ChatGPT, and they're still that way after launch. I'm really excited about the little things they've been doing to make the experience less buggy and more complete, and I think it'll get even better over the next couple weeks. What's been really interesting, though, is seeing the team at Every.
Speaker 1 | 00:46 - 01:20 We've got about 30 people seeing them start to adopt it and some of the use cases that have started to emerge. So in case you're looking for some use cases, I actually had my dot collect some use cases to talk to you about. So one thing that dots are really useful for is keeping up with school emails. So Kieran Klassen, who works at Every, says that it scans all of the school emails he gets from his kid's school and tells him what he needs to know. Another thing that DOTS are really good for is catching access requests or, like, little things, little messages you might have missed in Slack and making sure that you get them.
Speaker 1 | 01:20 - 02:04 So Ariel Shipper, our head of operations, heard Dot caught a few people asking for different accounts across the company and asked if she wanted it to just approve access. Dots are also really good for working when you're not at your computer or your hands are full. So our head of video, Randy Kunzman, was running around yesterday trying to get our launch video out for the Every Agent which launched, and he was doing work for that launch just on the phone with his dot, talking it through different video edits and different things he needed to get done. I also think this is something that came up in my interview with Sam, and I I feel this too. Dots are really good for filtering out all of the noise that you don't really want to see and only showing you stuff that really matters.
Speaker 1 | 02:04 - 02:43 So for example, I was doing a lot of model testing over the weekend, and normally, testing requires me to be in the every Slack, which once I'm in Slack, it's just like this rabbit hole of I'm just going down doing tons and tons and tons of work. And what was amazing about using my dot doing model testing was I was able to post the results of all the experiments I was running in Slack. And if someone responded, that my dot would tell me about the response, which would help me stay up to date on what the team was thinking without getting me sucked into the whole rabbit hole of everything going on in Slack. And that helped keep my weekend pretty clear and calm. And I think that's a huge, huge thing for dots.
Speaker 1 | 02:43 - 03:05 So what's the overall vibe? If you don't have a dot, I highly recommend you get one, especially if you're in the Chachapati ecosystem. If you're using Muse or Instinct or Grockbots, you should check it out. I think that they're pretty much at feature parity right now, but there's something really good about having something that's hooked into the entire rest of the ecosystem that you use for your work and your life. There are still rough edges, though.
Speaker 1 | 03:05 - 03:30 The whole permission structure of DOTS is, like, completely a mystery to me and is extremely annoying. So for example, I often have to give multiple approvals to my DOT to do something basic, and even when I give it approval, it says it can't do it. So they really need to figure that stuff out to make the experience awesome. But I would expect in a year, this is the default way that you're interacting with all your AIs. You're probably not going to have it be a cute character.
Speaker 1 | 03:30 - 03:47 That would be my other, like, little hot take. Mine is named Boo. He's super cute. But my experience using Open Claws and other named agents like this is that as soon as something better comes along, you throw away the cute little character you develop. So my guess is I'll be using a persistent agent in in a year, but Boo will probably be dead.
Speaker 1 | 03:47 - 04:10 RIP Boo. We've also actually been working on our own persistent agent that's not a personal agent. It's a company agent, and that's actually come from this whole journey we've been on starting with open clause inside of every... And everybody having a personal agent and realizing how valuable it was for the company to have a personal agent. So we built one for ourselves, and then we just released it to all of our subscribers.
Speaker 1 | 04:10 - 04:44 So I brought Willie Williams on, our head of platform, who was instrumental in bringing the agent to life to talk about personal agents versus company agents, what it's like to build an agent at the frontier right now, and what that means for engineering teams going forward. I hope you enjoy. Willie, welcome to the show. Oh, thank for having me. For people who don't know, you are the head of platform.
Speaker 1 | 04:44 - 05:17 You are one of the driving forces behind the Every Agent, which we... Well, by the time this comes out, we'll have launched. Launching And I want to talk to you about the whole agent phenomenon. Because I think we're in this world right now where personal agents are the hot thing. And there's like a little bit of Groundhog's Day for me, I assume for you, because we went through our personal agent phase, like, nine months ago or eight months ago with the original Open Claw phase, and I feel like we learned a lot from that.
Speaker 1 | 05:17 - 05:45 And then now I feel like there's this whole new era of people who are experiencing the same thing and maybe will learn the same lessons. We for us, we went from Open Claw, everyone in the company's got a personal agent to we have a company agent and we liked the company agent so much that we actually just made a company agent for other people to use. But I want to just talk about that and try to talk about it as honestly as we can because it's possible we're wrong. Yeah. But I do think we've learned some things that are important.
Speaker 1 | 05:45 - 05:53 Maybe let's start with Open Claw because we actually disagreed and I think you ended up being right. Tell

Speaker 2 | 05:58 - 06:10 Well, think the funniest thing was, actually at the time, it was called Claudius? Claudius? Claudius. It was like the earlier version before... Because it was Clawbot, right?

item.title: What should an ambitious software engineer do today? Ten years ago, being a great software engineer gave you an unusual advantage: a rare skill you could apply to almost any industry. You could build a payments company, improve how hospitals operated, or create a new way for people to communicate....
item.description:
作者：Aditya Agarwal 账号：@adityaag 简介：General Partner @SPC, Co-Founder @Bevel_Health | Ex: Early Eng @facebook, CTO @Dropbox, Board @Flipkart | Optimist, Builder, Dad
What should an ambitious software engineer do today?
Ten years ago, being a great software engineer gave you an unusual advantage: a rare skill you could apply to almost any industry.
You could build a payments company, improve how hospitals operated, or create a new way for people to communicate. The same underlying ability opened doors into wildly different businesses.
Software was eating the world, and knowing how to build it gave you a seat at the head of almost every table.
“Get really good at software engineering” was remarkably versatile advice. You could acquire the skill first and figure out where to apply it later.
AI is making the ability to produce working software much more widely available. People who couldn’t have built a product a few years ago can now get surprisingly far. Experienced engineers can attempt projects that previously required a team.
Great engineering is still rare. But “I can build it” is becoming a weaker answer to why you, specifically, have an advantage.
The way I see it, there are three paths.
1. Go work on the thing that’s eating software
Help create the technology that is making software engineering more accessible.
That could mean AI research, or the infrastructure, systems, and tools needed to make new capabilities useful. Find problems where technical ability remains a serious constraint, and where solving them expands what other people can do.
2. Find a world-class domain expert and team up
Someone who has spent fifteen years in an industry may know where the expensive mistakes happen, why previous attempts to fix them failed, and who would buy a solution. That knowledge is hard to acquire from the outside.
At SPC, we’re seeing more people become promising founders without much prior software engineering experience. They bring deep domain knowledge and strong instincts about what needs to exist.
These are people worth getting to know. A great engineering partner can see possibilities they haven’t considered and help build something neither person could have imagined alone.
3. Write vanilla code… by shepherding a bunch of agents
This is the direction I find least compelling: doing roughly the same work inside a company, except now you supervise coding agents.
There will be valuable jobs like this. But if your ambition extends only to completing the same backlog faster, you’re underusing the moment.
I’d still get very good at engineering. Then I’d be deliberate about what that ability sits next to: a technical frontier that needs advancing, or deep knowledge of a problem worth solving.
Use the fact that you can build more to take responsibility for something bigger.
